newsitem.title: USA: Great Western may seek merger to avoid takeover.
newsitem.headline: Great Western may seek merger to avoid takeover.

text.p: Great Western Financial Corp. will likely talk with other savings and loans and banks about a possible merger to avoid a hostile takeover by the nation's largest thrift, H.F. Ahmanson.

Industry analysts expect a bidding war to emerge for Great Western, the nation's second largest thrift, as Ahmanson's $6.3 billion bid put in play a valuable property in the consolidating California thrift market.
On Monday night, Ahmanson offered to swap 1.05 of its shares for each Great Western share, valuing Great Western at about $45.28 a share based on Wednesday's share price.
"We've not seen the end of the bidding by any stretch of the imagination," said Jeff Naschek of Salomon Brothers, who believes Washington Mutual Inc. could bid about $50 a share for Great Western.
"I think Washington Mutual could bid that high and still show earnings accretion," Naschek said, adding, "for that matter, I think Ahmanson still has room to go on its bid."
Seattle-based Washington Mutual, which recently acquired Keystone Holdings Inc. and Keystone unit, American Savings Bank, declined comment.
David Berry, an analyst with Keefe Bruyette Woods, also thinks Washington Mutual would be a likely rival bidder.
"They've been explicit about their desire to expand in California," he said. "But it's uncertain if it can match Ahmanson."
Ahmanson's Chief Executive Officer Charles Rinehart said on Tuesday he believed Ahmanson's offer was compelling as it stands, but did not rule out raising the bid.
Great Western added nothing Wednesday to its statement on Tuesday that it was reviewing Ahmanson's offer.

Both companies are based in Los Angeles. A merger of the two, whose operations overlap, would allow Ahmanson to close 100 or more branches and realise savings of about $400 million. Experts said that few suitors could provide the cost savings Ahmanson can offer.
"It's the ultimate hand-in-glove merger due to the dramatic overlap, cost savings and synergies," said Charlotte Chamberlain, an analyst with Jefferies and Co.
Another potential bidder is Minneapolis-based First Bank System Inc., which lost a bitter battle against Wells Fargo and Co. for First Interstate Bancorp.
First Bank System declined comment as did other potential suitors Norwest Corp. and NationsBank Corp. Washington Mutual also declined comment.
Great Western stock rose 12.5 cents to $45 and Ahmanson's fell $1.75 to $43.125 in composite trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
"The stocks are trading in a way that is suggesting a third party might emerge," said one takeover specialist.
